newsitem.title: USA: Wash. state governor signs welfare reform.
newsitem.headline: Wash. state governor signs welfare reform.

text.p: Washington State Thursday joined the dozens of states that have radically overhauled their welfare systems to conform with new federal law.

Democratic Gov. Gary Locke signed into law a Republican-authored bill that requires welfare recipients to look for work, perform community service or attend job training as a condition of receiving a check. Under the bill, which takes effect in 90 days, welfare recipients can collect for no more than five years over a lifetime.
"Tonight we've reached a historic milestone," said Locke, as he ended 60 years of state welfare entitlement with the stroke of his pen.

"With its clear and single-minded focus on work as the escape route from poverty, and because of its fairness to all people including immigrants, this legislation restores the American dream for the poorest of the poor."
The legislation restores welfare benefits and food stamps to legal immigrants who are being cut off of federal support. That will cost the state $115 million over the next two years.

State budget writers assume the new welfare requirements will reduce the public assistance caseload by 15 percent by 1999. Other states have seen even greater reductions after imposing strict work requirements. In Washington state, the welfare caseload has already started to fall -- most likely due to the state's strong economy.
Washington is the latest state to overhaul its welfare program to conform with federal welfare reform signed into law by President Clinton last August.

Advocates for the poor had called on the governor to veto the welfare reform bill. But last-minute concessions from the Legislature and selective section vetoes by the governor softened their concerns.
